clue.text: Wear, once a river with just one fish

parts.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge
I is the Roman numeral for one
the sole is a flatfish

explanation.surface: An odd tale of a river holding only a single fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks the garment as old-fashioned: the word once named a short sleeved jacket as well as a vest-like bodice.
explanation.definitionFit: A light bodice or underbodice is a garment, an item of clothing worn, chiefly in earlier days.

clue.text: Paperwork dodged by skiver

explanation.surface: Office paperwork that a work-shy employee avoids.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'column-dodger' was old military slang for a shirker, so the thing a skiver dodges is this word.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper piece is a regular feature written for a paper; and a column-dodger is service slang for a skiver avoiding the march.

clue.text: Proposal of marriage one tries it out nervously initially

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the words that run from marriage to nervously

explanation.surface: A nervous suitor rehearses a marriage proposal before popping the question.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal suggestion put before a meeting for debate is a proposal.

clue.text: Sally conceals support for divination

indicators.note: conceals means one word wraps round and covers the other

parts.note: a sally is a sudden sortie by troops from a besieged place
a leg is a support, as of a table

explanation.surface: A sudden military raid hides some prop used for fortune-telling.
explanation.definitionFit: Casting lots to foretell the future is a form of divination or sorcery.

clue.text: Raises a rifle, resolved to have no interference

indicators.note: resolved here means broken up and rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: Someone lifts a gun, determined that nobody shall meddle with them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' looks like determination in the surface, but it signals the letters of RAISES A RIFLE being worked into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: A hands-off policy of letting things take their own course means no interference by government.

clue.text: I'll be blest if I do it!

definitions.text: I'll be blest if I do it!

parts.words: I'll be blest if I do it!
parts.note: an exclamation of refusal, read literally: after doing this action people say 'bless you'

explanation.surface: A stubborn person flatly refusing to do something.
explanation.definitionFit: After this involuntary nasal explosion, bystanders traditionally say 'bless you'.

clue.text: Young woman gives heartless refusal with speed

indicators.note: heartless means the middle letter of the word is removed

parts.note: nay is an old word of refusal
mph, miles per hour, is a measure of speed

explanation.surface: A girl turns someone down coldly and in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the middle A out of NAY to leave NY.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry and myth a beautiful maiden is called by this name for a nature spirit.

clue.text: Object with passion to compromise

parts.note: an end is an object or aim
anger is a strong passion

explanation.surface: Someone protests vehemently in order to make a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: To put in danger or expose to risk is to compromise someone's safety.

clue.text: Close finish this man batting in breathless hush

definitions.text: Close finish this man batting in breathless hush

parts.words: Close finish this man batting in breathless hush
parts.note: recalls Newbolt's 'There's a breathless hush in the Close tonight', where the last man in must win the cricket match

explanation.surface: A tense end to a school cricket match with the final batsman in.
explanation.walkthrough: Newbolt's poem Vitai Lampada describes a school cricket match in 'the Close', with ten to make and the last man in; in cricket the last of eleven batters goes in at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: In a cricket team of eleven, the last batsman in holds this ordinal position.

clue.text: Settled most of press, in charge of services

parts.note: lit, as a bird lit on a branch, means settled or alighted

indicators.note: most of means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to urge someone is to press them

explanation.surface: A clergyman takes charge of church services after a quarrel with the press is settled.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to set forms of public worship means concerning church services.

clue.text: Smear with insect repellant

explanation.surface: Someone daubs on midge cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A blot or smudge is a smear; and a smoky fire lit to drive off gnats is also given this name.

clue.text: It can take you unawares

parts.note: read as a device that photographs you without your knowing, and the TV show built on pranking people secretly

explanation.surface: A warning that something may catch you by surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' is the photographic sense; the answer was a TV show filming people secretly.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden camera films people who do not know they are being recorded, as in the prank TV show.

clue.text: May, abroad, see nothing right in a native

indicators.note: in means the letters go inside the other word

parts.note: mai is the French for the month of May
O is the figure for nothing

explanation.surface: In May overseas, a traveller sees nothing quite right about a local.
explanation.definitionFit: A Polynesian of New Zealand is an indigenous inhabitant, a native of those islands.

clue.text: Transformation in mermaid's purse?

explanation.surface: A strange metamorphosis found inside a mermaid's purse.
explanation.walkthrough: A mermaid's purse is really the egg case of a skate; read as a purse for coins, its contents would be change from the sea. The phrase comes from Ariel's song in The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: A profound alteration or transformation; punningly, the coins a sea-dweller might carry.

clue.text: Coming back up rough track, following engineers

indicators.note: following means the later pieces come after the engineers in the answer

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers
crude means rough or unrefined
a scent is a track followed by hounds

explanation.surface: A rough trail, after the engineers have passed, is reappearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaking out again after a period of quiet, as a disease returns, is coming back up.

clue.text: Change down into first, perhaps, for road hazard in winter

indicators.note: change means the letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A driver changes down into first gear because of dangerous winter roads.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a gear change; 'Change' signals rearranging the letters of DOWN and FIRST together, and 'into' and 'perhaps' just link.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank of wind-blown snow blocking a road is a winter hazard for motorists.

clue.text: Not even dances will do for Nonconformists

parts.note: an odd number is one that is not even
balls are formal dances

explanation.surface: Uneven dances are enough for religious dissenters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric people who do not fit in are nonconformists.

clue.text: Pen bad child up — no, sir!

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A parent shuts a naughty child away despite the protest 'no, sir!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns NO SIR backwards to give RISON.
explanation.definitionFit: To pen someone is to shut them in, confine or lock them up.

clue.text: Family novel soon, by demand, to be translated

indicators.note: to be translated means turned into another form, here a new order of letters

explanation.surface: A family saga, by popular demand, is soon to appear in translation.
explanation.walkthrough: Dombey and Son is a novel by Dickens about a father and his children.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's book centres on a merchant and his children, a novel about a family.

clue.text: Poor artist's hardship

indicators.note: poor signals the word in bad shape, its letters scrambled

parts.note: the possessive adds no letters

explanation.surface: A starving artist knows real hardship.
explanation.definitionFit: In the plural, dire straits are difficulties; a strait is a position of distress or hardship.

clue.text: Sang-froid of Hull's first member admitted by PM

indicators.note: admitted by means the pieces are let inside the other word

parts.note: PM, the Prime Minister, taken as written

indicators.note: first picks out the opening letter of Hull's

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A Hull MP is admitted to see the Prime Minister and shows cool composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hull's first' is a pick of one letter, not the city; 'admitted by' puts the limb word and that letter inside the Prime Minister's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm composure or coolness under pressure is called sang-froid, the old phlegmatic humour.

clue.text: Island where two nautical chaps returned with a song

indicators.note: returned means each sailor's word is turned back to front

parts.note: an AB, able seaman, is a sailor
a tar is an old word for a sailor
an aria is a song in opera

explanation.surface: Two sailors come back to an island singing a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns each sailor word round where it stands, rather than swapping their order. Barataria is the island Sancho Panza governs in Don Quixote.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cervantes, the governorship given to Sancho Panza is an imaginary island.

clue.text: One who pronounces judgment on the Moselle

explanation.surface: A judge living beside a German river.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tries a case pronounces judgment; and Trier is an old German city standing on the Moselle.

clue.text: Drop in the ocean

explanation.surface: The proverbial drop in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Ditch' is slang for the sea, especially the Atlantic or the Tasman.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to drop or abandon it; and the Ditch is slang for the sea.

clue.text: Dog star (not Sirius)

parts.note: not the bright star in Canis Major but a canine film celebrity, the collie of the movies

explanation.surface: Astronomy quiz: name the dog star, and it isn't Sirius.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous rough collie of film and television was a canine star.

clue.text: What's left when Monsieur leaves solitary cell

indicators.note: leaves means the letter goes away from the word

parts.note: a hermitage is a hermit's solitary dwelling

explanation.surface: A Frenchman walks out of solitary confinement.
explanation.definitionFit: What is handed down to later generations is an inheritance, what predecessors left behind.

clue.text: Man watching three-quarters score at Twickenham

parts.note: three of the four compass quarters, South, East and North
a try is a score in rugby, and Twickenham is England's rugby stadium

explanation.surface: Rugby three-quarters score a try at Twickenham.
explanation.walkthrough: Three-quarters are rugby backs, but here they are three of the four compass points. Twickenham is the London home of English rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier on guard duty is a man watching over a post.

clue.text: Chap like Figaro, in truth, turned out married

parts.note: a fact is a truth

indicators.note: turned means the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man like Figaro, it turns out, is in fact married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' rearranges OUT into OTU. Figaro sings 'Largo al factotum' in The Barber of Seville.
explanation.definitionFit: Figaro is a barber and jack-of-all-trades, a general handyman or servant.
